name: Habsburg-Lorraine
summary: The marriage of Maria Theresa and Francis Stephen continued the Habsburg monarchy through a new family line.
origin: Francis Stephen was Duke of Lorraine and married Maria Theresa of Habsburg in 1736. The international negotiations that made the marriage possible forced him to surrender Lorraine. In compensation, he received Tuscany in 1737 after the death of the last Medici grand duke.
history: Maria Theresa inherited her father’s lands in 1740 and defended her rights during the War of the Austrian Succession. Francis was elected emperor in 1745. Their sons Joseph II and Leopold II later assumed both the imperial dignity and government of the hereditary lands.
legacy: The family promoted administrative, fiscal and religious reforms during the eighteenth century. Its marriages connected Vienna with France, Naples, Parma and other courts. Francis II faced the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars, adopted the title Emperor of Austria in 1804 and relinquished that of Holy Roman Emperor in 1806. The house continued to rule from Vienna.

name: Nassau
summary: Rhenish counts who divided into two branches in 1255: the Walramian line, which produced a King of the Romans and the grand dukes of Luxembourg, and the Ottonian line, which inherited lands in the Netherlands and the Principality of Orange.
origin: The counts of Laurenburg built Nassau Castle beside the Lahn in the twelfth century and took its name. In 1255, the sons of Henry the Rich divided the county: Walram founded the Walramian line and Otto the Ottonian line.
history: Adolf of Nassau, from the Walramian branch, was King of the Romans from 1292 to 1298. In the Ottonian branch, Engelbert I inherited lordships in the Netherlands during the fifteenth century, and the Nassau-Dillenburgs served the dukes of Burgundy and the Habsburgs. In 1544 William, son of William the Rich, inherited the Principality of Orange from his cousin René of Chalon.
legacy: William of Orange led the Dutch Revolt against Philip II, and his descendants became stadtholders of the United Provinces; William III was also king of England, Scotland and Ireland from 1689. The Nassau-Dietz branch inherited the headship of the house, and in 1813 William I received the throne of the Netherlands together with the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg.

name: Oldenburg
summary: A German comital house that united Denmark and Norway, contested Sweden and divided into numerous ducal branches.
origin: Christian I descended from the counts of Oldenburg. His election in Denmark in 1448 opened a new period after the death of Christopher of Bavaria. He married the widowed queen Dorothea of Brandenburg, strengthening continuity at the Danish court.
history: Christian united Norway with Denmark and reigned in Sweden for several years. His sons John and Frederick held different positions within the family domains. The deposition of Christian II brought his uncle Frederick I to the throne, while Sweden elected Gustav Vasa. Under Christian III, the Reformation transformed the institutions of Denmark and Norway.
legacy: The Schleswig-Holstein branches and their offshoots extended the family’s presence across several European monarchies. After Norway separated from Danish government in 1814, the Oldenburgs continued to reign in Denmark.

name: Ottoman
summary: The dynasty of Osman ruled from Anatolia over an empire that took Constantinople in 1453 and expanded across the Balkans, the Middle East and North Africa.
origin: Osman I was a frontier leader in north-western Anatolia at the beginning of the fourteenth century. His successors took Bursa and crossed into Europe; Murad I expanded through the Balkans, while Bayezid I was defeated and captured by Timur at Ankara in 1402, opening a decade of war among his sons.
history: Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453 and made it his capital. Selim I incorporated Syria and Egypt in 1516–1517, and Suleiman the Magnificent reached Hungary, Baghdad and the western Mediterranean. With no rule of primogeniture, succession was often resolved by eliminating the new sultan’s brothers.
legacy: From the late sixteenth century, much government passed to viziers, including the Köprülüs, and to the imperial harem. The failure before Vienna in 1683 opened a period of retreat in the Balkans, sealed by the Peace of Karlowitz in 1699. Selim III attempted to modernise the army in the late eighteenth century.

name: Palaiologos
summary: The last imperial dynasty of Constantinople ruled a shrinking state while maintaining family connections across the Mediterranean.
origin: The Palaiologoi appear among Byzantine military families from the eleventh century. Michael VIII gained power at Nicaea and, after recovering Constantinople in 1261, established his dynasty there. His government gathered resources through alliances with Genoa and negotiations with other Mediterranean powers.
history: Andronikos II and his successors faced civil wars, territorial losses and financial difficulties. Marriages with Armenian, Serbian, Bulgarian and Latin families formed part of their diplomacy. Several members also ruled the Despotate of the Morea, while one branch inherited the Marquisate of Montferrat.
legacy: Manuel II and John VIII sought western aid against the Ottoman advance. Constantine XI died during the conquest of Constantinople in 1453. The Morea fell in 1460 and several family members took refuge in the West. The Montferrat branch continued to rule in Italy into the sixteenth century.

name: Estridsen
summary: The final generation of the old Danish house carried its rights into Norway, Mecklenburg and the Kalmar Union.
origin: The house takes its name from Estrid and the descendants of Sweyn II. Its connections with Norway and Mecklenburg became especially important during the succession crises of the late Middle Ages.
history: Ingeborg, daughter of Erik IV, was the mother of the Norwegian kings Erik II and Haakon V. Later, Valdemar IV’s daughters opened two different paths: Margaret had Olaf with Haakon VI, while her sister Ingeborg married Henry of Mecklenburg and became the grandmother of Erik of Pomerania.
legacy: After Olaf’s death, Margaret promoted Erik of Pomerania, the grandson of her sister Ingeborg, while preserving her own authority. Through his father Erik belonged to the Griffin dynasty and through his mother descended from the family of the old Danish kings.

name: Mecklenburg
summary: The descendants of the Obotrite princes maintained a Baltic dynasty that also reached the Swedish crown.
origin: The ducal house descended from the Slavic princes of the Obotrites. Their successors consolidated Mecklenburg within the Holy Roman Empire and took part in the Christianisation and colonisation of the region. In 1348 Albert II and his brother John were elevated to ducal rank.
history: Albert, son of Albert II, was elected king of Sweden in 1364. His defeat by Margaret of Denmark in 1389 ended that branch’s rule in Sweden. In the German lands, family partitions produced several lines, including Schwerin and Güstrow.
legacy: The Reformation and the Thirty Years’ War altered the balance among the dukes, nobility and towns. The settlement of 1701 established the Schwerin and Strelitz lines. Marriage alliances extended the family’s influence: Sophia became queen of Denmark, Charlotte queen of Great Britain and Louise queen of Prussia.

name: Hohenstaufen
summary: The lords of Staufen attained the crowns of Germany and Sicily and fought a prolonged struggle for imperial authority in Italy.
origin: The house rose when Frederick of Staufen received the Duchy of Swabia and married Agnes, daughter of Henry IV, in 1079. Conrad III was elected king in 1138. His nephew Frederick Barbarossa gained the crown in 1152 and was crowned emperor in 1155.
history: Henry VI, Barbarossa’s son, married Constance of Hauteville and conquered the Kingdom of Sicily in 1194. Their son Frederick II combined the imperial dignity with rule in Sicily. Conflict with the papacy and the Italian cities marked his reign and those of his successors.
legacy: Conrad IV died in 1254. Manfred ruled Sicily until his defeat and death at Benevento in 1266; Conradin was executed after the campaign of 1268. Women of the house transmitted rights and connections to other families: Manfred’s daughter Constance married Peter III of Aragon, and Beatrice of Swabia married Ferdinand III of Castile.

name: Barcelona-Sicily
summary: The Sicilian branch of the House of Barcelona maintained the island’s political separation from Angevin Naples.
origin: Peter III of Aragon took the Sicilian crown after the Vespers of 1282, supported by the rights of his wife Constance, Manfred’s daughter. Their son James inherited Sicily and later Aragon. The Treaty of Anagni in 1295 envisaged returning the island to Angevin rule.
history: Sicilian representatives proclaimed James’s brother Frederick king in 1296. The Peace of Caltabellotta in 1302 recognised his rule under the title King of Trinacria. The succession continued through his descendants amid conflict with Naples and the island’s great families.
legacy: Peter II, Louis and Frederick the Simple ruled amid aristocratic rivalry and family regencies. Mary inherited the crown in 1377 and married Martin the Younger of the Aragonese branch. When both died without a surviving successor, government passed to Martin the Humane and became tied to the general succession of the Crown of Aragon.

name: Champagne
summary: A comital house from northern France whose connections extended to Navarre, Brittany and the eastern Mediterranean.
origin: The counts of Champagne belonged to the house of Blois. Their marriages connected them with Navarre, Brittany, Jerusalem and Cyprus.
history: Theobald III married Blanche of Navarre. Their son Theobald I inherited Champagne and, in 1234, the Navarrese crown. Another daughter of Theobald I, Blanche of Champagne, married John I of Brittany. Through another branch, Henry II of Champagne and his daughter Alice linked the house to the kingdoms of Jerusalem and Cyprus.
legacy: Joan I inherited Navarre and Champagne and married Philip IV of France. Their sons united the French and Navarrese crowns. In 1328 Joan II inherited Navarre, while Philip VI of Valois succeeded in France.

origin: Louis I, son of John II of France and brother of Charles V, received Anjou as an appanage and became duke in 1360. Joan I of Naples adopted him as her heir in 1380, originating this Valois branch’s Neapolitan claim.
history: Louis I and Louis II contested the Kingdom of Naples with the Durazzos. René combined inheritances and rights in Lorraine, Bar and Provence but lost Naples to Alfonso V in 1442. legacy: The house’s arms combined its hereditary lands with its claims to the titles of Naples and Jerusalem. The red bordure of Valois-Anjou distinguished it from the label used by the first Capetian Angevins.

name: Butler
summary: An hereditary office serving the lord of Ireland gave rise to one of the leading Anglo-Irish houses, associated with the Earldom of Ormond and Kilkenny Castle.
origin: Theobald Walter received the office of chief butler of Ireland in the late twelfth century. His descendants adopted the name Butler and built an extensive network of estates and marriages.
history: The title Earl of Ormond was granted in 1328. Kilkenny became the family’s centre in the late fourteenth century. In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, disputes over the inheritance after Thomas, tenth earl, favoured the rise of the Kilcash branch.
legacy: James, first Duke of Ormond, defended the Stuarts during the seventeenth-century wars and again held responsibilities in Ireland after the Restoration. The family’s titles, estates and religious choices followed different paths; its history combines royal service with local aristocratic power.

name: Barberini
summary: A Tuscan family that reached the centre of papal power under Urban VIII and left a substantial artistic and bibliographical legacy in seventeenth-century Rome.
origin: The Barberini established themselves in Florence and later in Rome, where they accumulated wealth and curial offices. Maffeo’s election as Urban VIII in 1623 transformed their position.
history: The pope’s nephews pursued complementary careers: Francesco and Antonio became cardinals, while Taddeo married Anna Colonna and became Prince of Palestrina. Their palace, collections, library and artistic commissions accompanied the concentration of offices and property. Another Cardinal Antonio, the pope’s brother, was distinct from his namesake nephew.
legacy: The War of Castro and Urban VIII’s death in 1644 led to a crisis under Innocent X. The nephews sought refuge in France, but the family later recovered part of its position. Its libraries and collections prolonged an influence that did not depend solely on papal favour.

name: Carafa
summary: A house of the Neapolitan nobility with many branches, whose territorial, military and ecclesiastical power became especially prominent during the pontificate of Paul IV.
origin: The Carafa separated from the Caracciolo family during the Middle Ages. The family spread into many lines, including those known as della Spina and della Stadera.
history: From the fourteenth century, its members took part in the politics of the Kingdom of Naples and expanded their estates through service and marriage. Gian Pietro Carafa, elected Pope Paul IV in 1555, gave the house an exceptional position in Rome. That influence coexisted with the interests of its different Neapolitan branches.
legacy: Paul IV’s death in 1559 opened a serious crisis for his closest relatives. Other branches retained their aristocratic estates and pursued ecclesiastical and military careers in Naples and Rome.
